flagship.title: RoboSumo
flagship.lead: Two robots. A ring less than a metre across. Whoever leaves it first loses.
flagship.body: The most spectacular discipline of the championship, and the easiest one for a newcomer to grasp: the rules take a minute to explain, and winning comes down to engineering rather than budget. Several weight and size classes run in parallel, from simple builds for beginners to autonomous machines fielded by experienced teams.
flagship.point1Body: Push your opponent out of the ring. Everything else is regulation detail.
flagship.point2Body: Size and weight classes mean a first-timer and a seasoned team never meet in the same bracket.
flagship.point3Body: Bouts run over several rounds and draw the largest audience of the championship.

sumo.name: Robo Sumo
sumo.tagline: Push your opponent past the white border
sumo.summary: Two robots on a raised circular ring: you win when your opponent is the first to touch the surface outside the platform. Nine classes, from a 2.5 cm, 25 g Nano to a 3 kg Mega, autonomous and remote-controlled, including two-legged humanoids.
rules: A match runs to two wins out of three rounds. A round lasts 3 minutes; with no winner by then, the round is a draw.
After the whistle, autonomous robots wait 5 seconds before moving. Moving early hands the round to the opponent.
A robot may expand once the match starts, but it must remain one compact entity and never split into parts.
Shedding parts totalling more than 5 g loses the round. If both robots shed parts, the round is a draw.
Sticky traction compounds are banned: a tyre must not hold an 80 g/m² sheet of A4 for more than two seconds.
Downforce devices — vacuum pumps and magnets — are permitted in Mega Sumo only.
Mega, Mini, Micro and Nano start on the official RobotChallenge chip signal; without the chip the robot cannot compete.
scoring: The group stage is a round robin: 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss.
The knockout stage is best-of-three. The first team to win two rounds advances.
Humanoid Sumo scores inside the bout instead: a knock down is worth 2 to the opponent, a slip down 1, a push out 3.
In Humanoid, a robot that fails to get up within 10 seconds loses the bout immediately.
Teams level on group points are separated by their head-to-head result.

lineFollower.name: Line Follower
lineFollower.tagline: Three attempts, the fastest one counts
lineFollower.summary: The robot runs a closed course — a 15 mm black line on a white 2.8 × 4.5 m carpet — and returns to the start zone. Three classes: LEGO, open, and Enhanced, which adds a line gap, an obstacle and a seesaw.
rules: The event runs three rounds; the next round only starts once every team has completed the current one.
Each attempt has a 3-minute limit. A team that does not finish inside it is recorded as 03:00.001.
Once the robot crosses the start line it must be fully autonomous, otherwise the team is disqualified.
Envelope is 30 × 30 cm and up to 3 kg. A robot that fails inspection gets 5 minutes to be adjusted.
Leaving the line, spinning in place, reversing, or touching the timing equipment voids the attempt.
In Enhanced, briefly leaving the line to clear an obstacle is allowed, but the robot must return to the course and carry on.
LEGO Line Follower must be built from original LEGO parts; the only third-party items allowed are rubber bands holding cables.
scoring: Ranking is decided by the best — that is, the lowest — time across the three attempts.
A voided attempt and a robot leaving the carpet are both recorded as 03:00.001, not as a blank.
Timing comes from the electronic system triggered at the start line, not from a referee's stopwatch.
A result is valid only if the robot completed the whole course without leaving the line and the system captured a full time.

rugby.name: Robot Rugby
rugby.tagline: Three robots a side, three minutes
rugby.summary: A remote-controlled match on a 350 × 150 cm field with a 10 cm protective wall and try zones at each end. An oval 160 g rubber ball, a captain who can call a timeout, and rules built on the traditional game.
rules: A team fields up to 3 robots, one per team member; robots and members carry matching numbers 1–3.
Envelope is under 20 × 20 × 20 cm. Junior is up to 1.5 kg on LEGO EV3/NXT or VEX IQ controllers with at most 9 motors per team; Senior is up to 3 kg with no equipment restrictions.
Sucking in the ball, hiding it or fitting ball-holding devices is banned; extending parts must not exceed the ball's radius.
One 30-second timeout per match, called by the captain. Repairs happen only in the designated area during a stoppage, 30 seconds per attempt.
Touching a robot without the referee's permission is a yellow card. Two yellows for one member is a red, and the team plays on a robot short.
A robot that tips over or is pushed off the field may recover on its own or with help from teammates — play continues meanwhile.
scoring: A try is worth 1 point: the attacking team's robot has the ball and it touches the goal-line wall in the try zone.
A 5-point lead ends the match immediately in the leader's favour.
Disqualifying a team for a serious offence automatically awards the opponent 5 points.
Draws stand in the group stage; the knockout stage goes to extra time and a golden goal.
On level scores the referee compares both teams' cards, and the team with fewer wins.

droneSoccer.name: Drone Soccer
droneSoccer.tagline: 3 v 3 in the air, inside the net
droneSoccer.summary: A team event inside an enclosed 6 × 3 × 3 m netted arena. Each side flies one striker and two defenders, and the roles are fixed for the match. A goal counts when the striker's ball passes fully through the opponent's ring from the front.
rules: Drone size including the guard is 100 to 220 mm. Junior is up to 150 g, Senior up to 300 g including cover and battery.
Any controller model, but 2.4 GHz only. A team brings 3 competition drones and up to 3 spares.
Every drone carries an LED that switches between at least red and blue; the striker always shows its team's colour.
Defenders may not fully cross the halfway line into the opponent's half.
Collisions between drones are allowed. Metal propellers and sharp structural parts are banned.
A 30-second timeout is available in the knockout stage only — one per match, called by the captain.
Turtle Mode and other automatic self-righting systems are permitted after a fall.
scoring: Each goal is worth 1 point. Own goals do not count.
Group stage: 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss. The top two teams from each group advance.
After a goal, the scorer's striker must return behind the halfway line before the next attack — otherwise it is a penalty.
A penalty is taken within 5 seconds of the referee's signal, one striker against one defender; every other drone lands.
A drawn final or third-place match goes to three penalties a side.
Three red cards zero the team's score and hand the win to the opponent.

ringMaster.name: Ring Master Challenge
ringMaster.tagline: Rings on poles, multipliers and a sudden finish
ringMaster.summary: Five minutes on a 2 × 2 m field with twenty scoring poles. The robot places foam rings on poles worth 1, 2, 3 and 5 points; a yellow ring on top doubles that pole. Completing a diagonal or a square ends the match on the spot.
rules: Starting envelope is 25 × 25 × 25 cm and up to 2000 g. Once expanded the robot may not exceed 35 × 35 cm; height is unrestricted.
The robot may carry, grip or transport no more than 2 rings at a time.
Up to 4 drive motors and up to 4 manipulator motors, 12 V maximum, and the robot must move on wheels.
Control is wireless only. Junior builds from a construction kit; Senior has no restriction on materials or electronics.
The robot enters and leaves the yellow zone only through the 30 × 30 cm gate; rings may not cross the side boundaries.
A pole counts a maximum of 4 rings — anything above that is ignored.
The team removes its own disabled robot from the field, and the clock keeps running while it does.
scoring: The red and blue poles are worth 5 points each and accept only their own colour plus yellow rings.
Yellow poles are worth 1, 2 or 3 points per the official field map and are open to both teams.
A yellow ring on top of a coloured ring doubles the pole. Yellow on yellow adds no further multiplier.
Knocking an opponent's ring off is −10. Deliberately removing a ring, ramming a robot or damaging the field is a yellow card and −30.
Points are counted only after the final whistle, and only for rings seated securely on their poles.
Endgame — a diagonal or a square of fully scored poles — stops the match and wins it.

bowling.name: Robot Bowling
bowling.summary: An autonomous robot launches LEGO DUPLO balls down lanes at ten pins arranged in a triangle. A round is five frames and three minutes; a strike in the fifth frame opens lanes six and seven. Maximum score 150.
rules: Inspection envelope is 20 × 20 cm, expanding to no more than 30 × 30 cm. Height and weight are unrestricted.
Junior plays a 120 × 40 cm field with seven lanes, Senior a 160 × 60 cm field with five.
Every team plays 2 rounds of 5 frames; a frame allows up to two balls unless the first is a strike.
The ball may only be launched from the launch zone. Launching before entering it is a foul and the frame scores zero.
After a launch the robot must return to the start zone by itself; picking it up before its wheels touch the black line is a foul.
A ball that knocks pins after rebounding off the net or a side wall is a foul. So is the robot falling off the platform.
Teams get 30 minutes of debugging beforehand; the start zone and the robot's initial heading are announced before it begins.
scoring: A strike is 10 plus the pins from the next two balls. A spare is 10 plus the next ball.
An open frame is simply the pins knocked down by the two balls.
A strike in the fifth frame earns two bonus balls, played on lanes six and seven.
A fouled ball scores nothing; if the first bonus ball is a foul, the second is not given.
Ranking uses the average of the two rounds. Ties go to the better round, then to remaining time.

leap.name: Leap
leap.tagline: Build the festival stage in three minutes
leap.summary: A music-festival stage on a 0.9 × 2 m field: close the circuits, set the microphones, raise the speakers, deploy the screen, bring the band on, then trigger lighting, sound and the camera crane. Some tasks are driven by remote, others must run fully autonomously.
rules: Participants are 12 years old or younger.
The robot is built from plastic interlocking blocks only — LEGO Spike Prime, EV3, VEX IQ, micro:bit and equivalents. 3D-printed parts are banned.
One controller and no more than 4 motors per robot. Sensor type and count are unrestricted.
The robot must fit the START area; there is no height or weight limit.
Task order is free: remote and autonomous tasks can be interleaved, and the robot may return to START to swap attachments.
During an autonomous task nobody may touch the robot, the controller or the field props until the robot returns to START on its own.
Teams get 60 minutes of debugging beforehand; a round lasts 3 minutes and there are two rounds.
scoring: The task sheet is worth 270 points, or 300 with the championship bonus task.
The time bonus is (remaining seconds ÷ round length) × 30 — up to 10% of the base sheet.
Every retry costs 5 points. A robot that sheds no parts earns 5.
Ranking uses the better of the two rounds; ties go to the team with more time remaining.
The referee crew tallies the sheet after the round, from the final state of the field.

application.body: Register your team in your chosen discipline and pay the entry fee. It takes a few minutes.

confirmation.body: The organising committee checks your team's details and emails you confirmation along with the discipline regulations.

preparation.body: Build your robot and write your program to the regulations. Answers to technical questions and breakdowns of previous seasons are published before the start.

techCheck.body: On site, judges check your robot against the regulations: dimensions, weight, safety. Minor issues can be fixed within a grace period.

qualification.title: Qualifying
qualification.body: Qualifying runs and bouts within your category. The result sets your position in the bracket.

final.title: Final

faq.title: Answered in advance
faq.subtitle: The things competitors, parents and teachers ask us most.

cost.q: What does it cost to take part?
cost.a: The entry fee is {amount} {currency} per team, not per person. It covers participation in every stage of your chosen discipline, certificates and access to the venue. Everything else — travel, accommodation and building your robot — the team plans for itself.

travel.q: We're from another region. How do we get there?
travel.a: The championship is held in Astana. Teams usually plan to arrive the day before so they can get through technical inspection without rushing. The exact venue address, directions and recommended arrival time are sent to confirmed teams along with the regulations.

accommodation.q: Is there help with accommodation for teams from out of town?
accommodation.a: Accommodation is being confirmed with the organising committee. Mention it when you submit your entry, with your city and the number of people, and we'll suggest options near the venue and tell you whether any special rates apply for teams.

skillLevel.q: We've never competed before. Should we still enter?
skillLevel.a: Yes. The championship is open to teams at any level, from students building their first robot to experienced university teams. Every discipline has age categories, and RoboSumo adds weight classes on top, so beginners never face champions.

rules.q: Where can we read the rules and technical requirements?
rules.a: The full regulations are published before entries open and can be downloaded from this page. They cover robot dimensions and weight, permitted components, the format of bouts, and the judging criteria for each discipline.

selection.q: How are teams selected for the international stage?
selection.a: Places at RobotChallenge go to the strongest robotics teams based on the final. The selection criteria and the number of places are published in the regulations before the championship begins — nothing is decided behind closed doors afterwards.

teamChanges.q: Can we change the team line-up after entering?
teamChanges.a: Yes. Until entries close, changes are made by writing to the organising committee with your reference. After the deadline, substitutions are considered individually and only for good reason.

refund.q: What if our team can't make it?
refund.a: Let the organising committee know as early as you can, quoting your reference. The refund terms for the entry fee, and whether the place can be passed to another team from your organisation, are set out in the terms of participation.

equipment.q: Do we need to bring our own equipment?
equipment.a: Yes. Teams bring their own robot, tools and spare parts. There is a pit area at the venue with workbenches and power; what the organiser provides is listed in each discipline's regulations.

deadline.a: {date}, inclusive. We'd suggest not leaving it late: places in some categories are limited, and no entries are accepted after the deadline.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: This policy explains what personal data is processed when you enter the AstanaTechCup championship, why, and how long it is kept.
privacy.draftNotice: Draft. This document was prepared as a starting point and must be reviewed by the organiser's legal counsel before publication, including for compliance with the Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 94-V on personal data and its protection.
privacy.s1Body: The data controller is the championship organiser, {organizer}. Contact details for data protection enquiries are published in the Contact section.
privacy.s2Body: When you submit an entry: the team and organisation name, region and city, the names and ages of team members, and the contact person's name, email, phone number and note. When you pay the entry fee, payment details are handled by the payment provider — this site neither receives nor stores card details.
privacy.s3Body: To register your team and admit it to the competition, to confirm the entry and stay in touch, to produce results and award documents, and to keep the service secure and free from abuse.
privacy.s4Body: The championship's main audience is schoolchildren. Data about participants under 18 is submitted by a legal guardian or with their consent; confirming this is a mandatory condition of entry.
privacy.s5Body: Entry data is retained for the duration of the championship and the reporting period that follows, after which it is deleted or anonymised. Specific periods are set out in the controller's internal policy.
privacy.s6Body: Data is never sold, and never passed to third parties for advertising. Limited access is held by the service providers needed to run the site: hosting, email delivery, the payment provider and the bot-protection service.
privacy.s7Body: You may request a copy of your data, ask for it to be corrected or deleted, and withdraw your consent to processing. Contact the organising committee quoting your entry reference.
privacy.s8Body: Essential cookies keep the registration form working and protect against request forgery. Analytics cookies are set only after explicit consent and can be declined without losing any site functionality.
privacy.s9Body: Data is transmitted over an encrypted connection, access to it is restricted, and actions on entries are logged. Personal data is never written to service logs in the clear.

terms.title: Terms of participation
terms.draftNotice: Draft. This document was prepared as a starting point and must be reviewed by the organiser's legal counsel and aligned with the official competition regulations.
terms.s1Body: These terms govern entry to and participation in the AstanaTechCup national technology championship. The organiser is {organizer}; the co-organiser is {coOrganizer}.
terms.s2Body: Teams of school and university students who meet the age categories of their chosen discipline may take part. Age limits and maximum team size are stated in each discipline's description and checked when the entry is submitted.
terms.s3Body: Entries are submitted through the form on this site up to and including {deadline}. An entry is accepted once the organising committee has confirmed it and the entry fee has been received.
terms.s4Body: The fee is {amount} {currency} per team, paid through the payment provider's secure page. Refund terms are set by the competition regulations; a team withdrawing should notify the organising committee in good time.
terms.s5Body: Participants must follow their discipline's regulations. Robots undergo a technical inspection against the requirements for dimensions, weight and safety. Non-compliance may result in exclusion until the issues are resolved.
terms.s6Body: Results are determined by the judging panel according to the criteria published in the regulations. The procedure for lodging and hearing appeals is set out in the competition regulations.
terms.s7Body: Photography and filming take place at the venue. Consent to publish material featuring your team is requested separately and has no bearing on admission to the competition.
terms.s8Body: The organiser may adjust the dates, venue and regulations, giving registered teams timely notice through the contact details provided in their entry.
